unit.title: Let the computer search: knapsack, routes, timetables

lesson.title: Try them all, or think ahead
lesson.subtitle: Brute force, greedy and dynamic programming

video.title: Try them all, or think ahead
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — your computer studies teacher (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — your maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph in the computer room beside a picture of a small truck and six crates.
scenes.animation: Crates slide toward the truck and stop at a weight bar.
scenes.narration: A truck for a village school can carry a thousand kilos, and there are six loads to choose from. Can you write a program that finds the best load, and knows it’s the best?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Try them all, or think ahead
scenes.narration: Today: let the computer search, by trying everything, or by thinking ahead.

scenes.visual: Six crates labelled with weight and points; a scale shows the 1,000 kg limit.
scenes.animation: Each crate lights up as it is named.
scenes.narration: Each load has a weight and points for how much the school needs it. Solar panels: six hundred kilos, forty-two points. Desks and books: five hundred kilos each. A water filter, footballs and chalk are lighter. The goal: the most points within a thousand kilos.

scenes.visual: A tree of in/out choices branches six times into 64 leaves.
scenes.animation: Branches split level by level; a counter reaches 64.
scenes.narration: The simplest search tries every possible load. Each item is in or out, six times over. That’s two to the six, sixty-four loads: a phone checks them in a blink.

scenes.visual: Code typed on a card; beside it, the number 13 shown as bits 001101 lighting three crates.
scenes.animation: Code types itself; bits flip as the mask counts.
scenes.narration: In Python, count from zero to sixty-three, and read each number in binary: bit i says whether item i is in. Add up the weight and points, and keep the best that fits.

scenes.visual: Three stacks of paper growing: 64, then a tower, then off the top of the screen.
scenes.animation: Stacks grow; the last one shoots past the frame.
scenes.narration: But every extra item doubles the work. Thirty items: over a billion loads. Sixty items: more than a billion billion. Brute force is sure, but it doesn’t scale.

scenes.visual: Two trucks side by side: greedy (solar, filter, chalk: 60) and best (desks, books: 65).
scenes.animation: Crates load into each truck; the totals count up.
scenes.narration: A greedy rule is fast: take the most points per kilo first. Solar panels go in, then whatever still fits: sixty points. But desks and books give sixty-five. The panels took space that two other loads fill better.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up two answers, 60 and 65. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Greedy says sixty points, and brute force says sixty-five. Which one is guaranteed to be the best?

scenes.visual: The answer ‘Brute force’ gets a check; then small trucks of 100, 200, 300 kg fill up one after another.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; small trucks fill in order.
scenes.narration: Brute force: it checked every load. But you can be sure without checking everything. Dynamic programming solves smaller trucks first: for each amount of room, either skip this item, or take it and fill the rest with an answer you already know.

scenes.visual: Code on a card above a grid that fills cell by cell.
scenes.animation: Cells fill left to right, row by row.
scenes.narration: Fill a table: one row per item, one column per hundred kilos of room. Each cell needs just two lookups in the row above. A hundred items is about a thousand cells, where brute force would never finish.

scenes.visual: Two schools at the end of one road; all the crates pile up at one gate.
scenes.animation: Crates roll toward one school; a question mark appears over the other.
scenes.narration: The points are someone’s opinion of what the school needs. Who decided solar panels are worth forty-two? If the truck served two schools, the best total might send everything to one. Ask who chose the points, and who is left out.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: the truck, the six loads, and the dynamic programming table with outlined cells.
scenes.animation: A finger taps each button; the outlined path lights up backwards.
scenes.narration: In the app, open “Pack the truck”. Pack greedily, then show the best load. Open the table under the results, and follow the outlined cells back from the corner.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph adds a seventh crate. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A friend adds a seventh load to the list. How many loads must brute force check now?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; three summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: A hundred and twenty-eight: every extra item doubles it. Remember: brute force is sure, but it explodes. Greedy is fast, but it can miss. And dynamic programming is sure and fast, because it reuses smaller answers.

scenes.visual: A student at home with a bag, a few objects on a kitchen scale, and a small table in a notebook.
scenes.animation: Objects go in and out of the bag; the table fills.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: pack your bag for a school trip. Give each thing a weight and points, set a limit, and find the best load three ways.

checkpoints.prompt: Greedy says 60 points; brute force says 65. Which is guaranteed to be the best?

options.text: Greedy: it takes the best value first
Brute force: it checked every load

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — brute force compared all 64 loads, so 65 is the best. Greedy only looked at value per kilo.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — only a method that rules out every other load can be sure. Brute force checked all 64.

checkpoints.prompt: A seventh load is added. How many loads must brute force check now?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — each new item is in or out, so the count doubles: 2⁷ = 128.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — one more item doubles the count, because every old load can now be with or without it: 2⁷ = 128.
